unique_feature: a lone cairn on the down's shoulder above Fallowfold, a rag tied to a stick in its top for the shepherds to read the wind by
story: When the rag on the cairn streams north the wind is off the ash, and the West Downs' shepherds bring the flocks in to Fallowfold's pond to wash the grey out of the fleeces before it settles.
hook: The rag has streamed north all week, and there has been no wind at all.

name: The Garrison Shrine
unique_feature: a Warden shrine at the roadside for the Tumbled Watch's lost garrison, a stone with nine names cut on it where the patrols stop
story: The Tumbled Watch fell in the Quiet Villages years because its garrison stopped being talked about. The Wardens raised this shrine where the road can see the fallen tower, and every patrol that passes says the nine names aloud.
hook: Somebody has hung the Tumbled Watch's own bell back on the frame, the bell the bandits took from it, and the bandits in the watch swear they still have it.

name: The Turned-Back Fire
unique_feature: the fire where Warden patrols rest after turning back at the Last Hearth; it went out when the last patrol left, and the cups are still set round it
story: Patrols on the grey side turn back at the Last Hearth and stop here for the night, the first fire on the Vale side, before they walk home. The rule is to leave the cups set round it, so the next patrol knows how many came back.
hook: One cup at the cold fire is full every morning, and warm.

name: The Gossip Stones
unique_feature: three stones by the Merrowby road where the Vale's women stop on market day to talk, each worn into a seat
story: Gossip is a kind of prayer, the Vale says, and this is where it is prayed. The three stones are the Vale's oldest seats, and whatever is said on them by noon is known in every kitchen from Wynstead to Tamwick by supper.
hook: Nobody has sat on the middle stone since spring, and anyone who does forgets what they were about to say.

name: The Lantern Hummock
unique_feature: a peat island shrine by the North Channel causeway, lantern poles round a stone and an old bell just under the water beside it
story: The reedfolk bury their dead in the water with a lantern. For the ones the water took and did not give back, there is no burial, so a lantern is lit for them here on the hummock, on the one night each year that it can be seen from Moreva.
hook: A lantern has been lit on the hummock for somebody who is still alive, and the reedfolk will not say whose.

name: The Settled House
unique_feature: the roofless stilt-house of a Moreva family whose stilts rotted under it, the house settled down onto the peat with one gable still standing
story: When a stilt-house's stilts rot the reedfolk do not rebuild it. They say the house has come down to meet the water, and the family moves, and the house is left to wait for the flood the Tide account promises.
hook: The family has come back to live in it, sitting up on the gable and the beams, waiting, they say, for the water to come up and take them out to where it went.

name: The Pushers' Stones
unique_feature: three leaning stones on the bank below the Eelweir, where whoever was pushed off the weir each autumn climbs out and leans to dry
story: Reedfolk and Lakefolk share the Eelweir by an agreement neither side has read, and every autumn one of them pushes one of the other into the Outfall. The stones are where the pushed climb out and lean, dripping, and are handed a cup by the pusher, which is also the agreement.
hook: This autumn nobody was pushed in, for the first time in anyone's memory, and both sides are frightened of what that means.

name: The Malting Floor
unique_feature: the roofless malting house below the Hanger where the Vale's barley was sprouted for Tamwick's brewers, one gable standing over the flagged floor
story: Before Cress Mill took the brewers' barley, it was malted here, spread on the flags and turned by hand until it sprouted. The house fell in when the malting moved, and the flags have been grassing over ever since.
hook: The floor has sprouted again this spring, barley coming up between the flags in the shape of a man lying down.

name: Toll View
unique_feature: a bench on a flagged plinth on the Stride road where the Cracked Toll is first seen whole, a cairn of bronze-streaked stones beside it
story: Travellers coming off the Long Stride stop here for their first sight of the Toll, the bronze bell forty metres tall and half sunk in the hill. The cairn is made of stones with bronze in them from where the crown broke, and the Vale is very proud of it.
hook: The bench hums when you sit on it now, since the Toll began to hum, and the old men of Stride's Foot who sit there have started humming back.

name: The Dole-House
unique_feature: the roofless dole-house below Hollin Barrow where the Barrow Reeve's alms were given out, one gable standing and a stone coffin inside it for the bread
story: The Barrow Reeve kept the barrow and gave alms at its foot, bread in a stone coffin that the poor lifted the lid of themselves, so nobody need be seen taking. The Reeve has been in the barrow a long time, and not resting, and the dole-house fell in.
encounter: a hedge-wight works the verge after dark
hook: Alms have been left in the stone coffin, bread and a penny, and in the morning the penny is gone and the bread is not.

name: The Quiet Mile
unique_feature: a waystone on the West Walk road cut with the names of the four quiet villages and a mile to each that nobody can walk
story: The Wardens set the stone so the names on the Roll are read by everyone who passes: Mullbourne, Harewell, Larkstead and Gosford, each with its mile cut beside it, though no road goes there any more and no map shows them.
hook: A fifth name has been cut below the four, fresh, and the Wardens have not struck any village from the Roll.

name: The Salt Road Cairn
unique_feature: a lone cairn on the grey heath where the salt-traders' road came up from the strand, each of its stones rimed white with old salt
story: The Salt Isles traders left a stone on the cairn going inland and took one back coming down to their boats, so the cairn stood a stone higher for every trader still ashore. They stopped coming forty years ago, and the cairn has been exactly as high since.
hook: A stone crusted with fresh salt has been added to the cairn, the first in forty years, and the Strand Beacon burned green that night.

name: The Last Meal Stone
unique_feature: a flat stone on the rim road where pilgrims eat their last meal as Vale folk before they go down, crusts and cups left round it
story: The pilgrims walking to the Choir stop being Vale folk at the Ninth Waystone and start being pilgrims, and at this stone they eat the last food they brought from home. What is left is left on the stone, and the knights of the ring clear it at dusk and say nothing.
hook: Somebody has eaten a last meal at the stone every evening this month, and in the morning the plate is washed and set straight, and nobody new is on the Stair.

name: The Bowing Stones
unique_feature: three leaning stones on the Choir road beneath the Headless Watch, bent toward the Choir like the colossi bowing
story: The Builders set three stones where their procession first saw the Choir whole, and the stones have leaned toward it ever since, a little more every century, the way the pilgrims lean when they first see it themselves.
hook: The stones have leaned a hand further toward the Choir since the Toll began to hum, and the knight in the Headless Watch's eye has measured it.

name: The Scavengers' Cold Camp
unique_feature: an Ashgrid scavengers' camp on the Greyfold road; the fire went out and nobody relit it, and sacks of Builders' brass are left by the cold hearth
story: The Ashgrid's scavengers dig brass out of the dead city for Tollmere's foundries and camp in the lee of whatever wall stands. This camp was left all at once, with the brass still in the sacks, which a scavenger does not do.
encounter: ash-wights wander the Greyfold road after dark
hook: Every piece of brass the scavengers left in their sacks has been polished bright in the night, as if for a feast.

name: The Robing-House
unique_feature: a Builders' robing-house beside the Anthem Hall, roofless, one gable standing, stone pegs down its walls for robes long gone to ash
story: The Builders' singers robed here before they went into the Anthem Hall, a peg for every singer, and the pegs are still there in rows. The pilgrims count them and count the Hall's benches, and the numbers match.
hook: Grey robes have been hung on the pegs, dry and newly woven and sized for children, one peg short of the Anthem Hall's benches.

name: The Harbour Milestone
unique_feature: a broken Oroth milestone on the harbour road, its top lying face-up at its foot, a ship cut on it and a count in Oroth numerals that nobody can read
story: The Builders' road from their city to their harbour was marked with stones, and this is the last one standing, or half standing. The Sayers read the numerals as a count of something, not a distance, and have argued for a century about what.
hook: The count on the fallen top has gone down by one since spring.

name: The First Verse
unique_feature: a waystone at the Dreughow road's last bend painted with the first verse of the Rope-Song, as Dreughow's doors are painted
story: Dreugh sing first at the Moot, and paint the first verse on their doors so a stranger knows the order of things before he knocks. The stone at the bend tells him before he reaches the doors, so he has the length of the road to learn it.
hook: The verse on the stone has been painted over in grey, the grey of the Hush, a word at a time, a word a night.
